en: Yuktipradīpa (Tucci manuscript), cf. Sankrtyayana 1937:27–28.
Input by Péter-Dániel Szántó, September 2012, Oxford (proofread only once).
Most of the text on the right side of the photographs is out of focus.
[Scribbled: *Yuktipradīpa*. This is the manuscript of the *Śrīguhyasamāja-maṇḍalopāyikā*, the *Bhramahara-sādhana*. Homage to the Buddha!
Having bowed my head with devotion to the multitude of pollen-dust from the lotus feet of the glorious Guru, who possesses eternally pure qualities;
I shall explain the lamp of reasoning that dispels the darkness of opposing views, which is the means for accomplishing the attainment of a supreme and virtuous friend.
As for those fools, stupefied by the entire web of conceptual constructions, who claim that Buddhahood is accomplished merely upon receiving the instructions of a genuine guru—
"O [x x x x], one who is engaged in worship need not perform daily rites and the like;
this much alone is indeed tolerated. [The question remains: Is Buddhahood established apart from activities such as meditation, or not?
[Objection: Surely enlightenment exists even for one devoid of activities such as meditation. How so?"
The recitation of the dhāraṇī-mantra is the cause of the delusion of all these; therefore,
one should not remain for even a moment in meditation with an impure mind.
Remaining in bliss, do not agitate yourself;

the mind itself is stainless. [Five syllables deleted] It is stainless and immaculate, devoid of the entire triad of subject and object, fear, shame, passion, hatred, greed, delusion, envy, jealousy, slander, cold, heat, hunger, thirst, sleep, sexual intercourse, the burning of fire, the flooding of water, the hardness of mountains and the like, as well as the turbidity born from the web of conceptual constructions regarding self and what belongs to the self.
"Even in a precipice... [the yogin] becomes... This was said with reference to a yogin established in the fourth stage, and not to beginners and others.
Furthermore, by means of mere conviction in reality (*tattva-adhimukti*), all virtuous action whatsoever must be performed. And so it was said by the venerable Nāgārjuna:
"Those who do not understand the meaning of solitude, relying merely upon what they have heard..."

"Those who do not perform meritorious deeds are slain; they are the lowest of men. (Yuktiṣaṣṭikā 31) What [is the meaning of the statement that] "like gold"? This too is not... for you. How so? Just as there might be the appearance of stainless gold once the state of being iron has been abandoned.

In the same way, having turned back the ordinary continuum (*prākṛtasaṃtāna*), he has become one endowed with the entire multitude of excellent qualities—such as the thirty-two marks of a Great Man and the eighty minor characteristics that adorn his body, the fathom-wide radiance, the divine sight, the divine hearing, the knowledge of others' minds, the recollection of former abodes, the power of divine miracles, the [ten] powers, the [four] grounds of self-confidence, and so forth. This is because of the non-arising of the grasped and the grasper, and so on.

Now, it might be argued that the water becomes clear upon entering the cavity of the pot, just as water becomes clear when entering a ring-shaped fruit. That too is inconsistent, because the previously mentioned impurities have not been removed. Merely by hearing the statement, "Water was brought after taking a jar fashioned from this lump of clay," who would be capable of bringing that very same water [in that state]? Furthermore, how could there not be the drying up of the water-thread from the time of the stick’s application until its removal?

Just as from the mere hearing that "the cessation of hunger occurs through eating food," the cessation of hunger is not actually perceived; likewise, by this very path, it is heard that "having gone to the Jewel Island and so forth, great jewels are obtained," yet they do not actually come to pass. In that regard, as long as one does not make an effort to go by embarking upon a ship and so forth, [the goal is not reached]. For indeed, how could a medicinal herb, merely by being mentioned, remove the disease of a sick person?
And so it is said in the *Bodhicaryāvatāra*:
"I shall practice with the body alone; what would be the use of verbal recitation? What will happen to a sick person by the mere recitation of a medical treatise? (BCA 5.109).

Furthermore, how does a yogin come to be counted among the Vajradharas upon attaining reality? To this it is said: there are two types of yogins—those of the fixed lineage and those of the unfixed lineage.

In this regard, one who belongs to the fixed lineage (*niyatagotra*) is designated as an *avadhūta*... because it was so stated by the Blessed One. Just as in the great ocean, having made that ship well-fastened with strong bonds and well-caulked, one who has boarded it—having released the sails and being free from the occurrence of adverse conditions—will certainly reach the intended destination of the aforementioned jewels; so too, in the great ocean of existence, the practitioner (*yogin*)... [is] the Great Yoga (*mahāyoga*). What...?

That very person, having ascended [to that state] through the grace of the feet of a true guru, is considered to proceed toward the jewel-island of great bliss (*mahāsukha*) in order to attain the jewels of the qualities of perfect enlightenment—if there were no obstacles such as the transgression of the *samaya* through disrespect toward the guru. "Ascending" refers to the actual performance of practices such as meditative cultivation, and not merely hearing about it; for mere hearing does not constitute ascending.

Now, one might object: "A boat fashioned from the wish-fulfilling tree (*kalpataru*) is capable of carrying one across; therefore, one should remain attached to merit once non-virtuous karma has been abandoned. Having reached the far shore of the wilderness of cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), even that should be abandoned. As it is said in the *Śrī Māyājāla-mahātantra*:
"From the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), merit should be relinquished; what need is there to mention non-merit?
Just as a being crossing to the other side of a river filled with water [leaves the boat behind]."

Having gathered wood and grass and made a raft upon the water, one who has become stuck there may cross over, leave it behind, and proceed with ease; even so, from the opposition of merit and demerit, one crosses to the further shore of saṃsāra.
"Enlightenment is attained with ease by one who is free from both dharma and adharma.

According to your position, whatever arises in the mind is all "innate play" (*sahajakrīḍā*). Consequently, even acts such as the taking of life—which are improper—would have to be performed within that play. This too appears to be invalid. If every act, including impure deeds and the like, were to become [pure] through innate play, then [such acts] would have to be accepted. Yet, deluded minds do accept them; this is precisely because they lack the conviction in right knowledge (*samyagjñāna-adhimokṣa*).

Whatever is an obscuration of unwholesome karma, all that leads only to cyclic existence (*bhava*). However, for one properly engaged in yoga, it bestows both mundane and supramundane fruits. That ordinary unwholesomeness, like a plantain tree, ceases after yielding its fruit. ... And the unsurpassed *bodhicitta* ... [is] the battle ... [is] the cause. As it has been said:
"One who practices non-reality through restrictive vows, fasts, recitations, and meditations will not attain accomplishment even in hundreds of millions of eons."
And so it was said by the venerable Nāgārjuna:
"For those who indeed desire the establishment of things in reality by means of dependence,
how could faults such as these not also apply to them?"
... essence ... equal to selflessness ... without incalculable eons (*asaṃkhyeya-kalpāḥ*), Buddhahood is not accomplished. As it is said in the *Samantabhadra*:
"Even though one is endowed with selflessness, [the practice of] giving and so forth (*dānādi*) [is performed] toward those who possess ordinary, innate forms."
For in this [state], there is no contradiction,
since there is neither becoming nor cessation.

Thus, water is carried by that jar; it is capable of being led to the desired place provided there is no misfortune such as being struck by a mallet or similar object. It is not, however, capable of being tied and led by one who is unripe or [unprepared]. And yet, you should speak thus:
"Without meditation, without recitation, while living in a house, the house will collapse."
"If one does not abandon them even while increasing one's indulgence in sense objects,
tell me, Saraha, what can such a person be called?"

"In vast, solitary forest regions and in mountain caves and groves, accomplishment is always attained"—thus it was said by the Blessed One. By relying on a place conducive to this meditation, one who is constantly and correctly engaged in yoga attains accomplishment even while living at home with a wife, despite the enjoyment of the five strands of sensual pleasure. [NB!]
"By enjoying all objects of desire as one wishes, through this very yoga, one shall indeed swiftly attain Buddhahood.
One should perform worship by means of the yoga of one's own tutelary deity and with the supreme limbs."
While enjoying all objects of desire as one wishes,
by means of this very yoga, one shall indeed swiftly attain Buddhahood.
"Success is not achieved by practicing difficult observances and hardships;

rather, success is quickly attained while enjoying all sensual pleasures," because this was specifically stated by the Omniscient One. And it was said by the venerable Indrabhūti: ... and it is further stated:
“Without meditation, without recitation,
and while living in a house, one is destroyed by the company of householders; if this is indeed true, O virtuous lady...”

"Alas! Fools, who would not find this pleasing? If it is argued that this must be so because of the purity of the yogin, one must ask: what kind of purity is that? [They claim that] through various modes such as meditation and recitation, they have attained, will attain, and are attaining nirvāṇa. But this is not so, because the total cessation of saṃsāra is never observed. Precisely for this reason, because its nature consists of profound and vast wisdom and skillful means (*prajñopāya*), one is eternally in a state of meditative absorption (*samāhita*) even through non-meditative yoga (*asamāhitayoga*). Furthermore, in the Great Mahāyāna, one achieves success in this very life. ...

Without obtaining the entire collection of all necessary materials—such as *sphoṭana*, *dūlaka*, *pañjikā*, *varttana*, *bhukkura*, *phalā*, and *masi*; as well as thread, string, water, clay, cloth, loom, staff, and so forth; and various implements such as sticks, small rods, *tuṇḍima*, and *maṇḍika*—the production of a manuscript would not be possible. But once it has been produced, that collection of materials...

Having obtained this entire collection—consisting of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, equanimity, generosity, ethical discipline, patience, vigor, meditative concentration, wisdom, skillful means, power, aspiration, and primordial cognition—enlightenment is accomplished in this very life. It does not arise through mere hearing alone, nor by relying on the vehicles of the Śrāvakas and others. Thus it was said by Bhadrapāda:
"Buddhahood does not come from conduct alone, nor does it arise from mere hearing; it is not attained even through reflection, but is said to result from meditative cultivation."

As for those non-Buddhist outsiders (*paratīrthika*) who maintain the existence of a soul (*jīva*) and so forth—they are like a painting of a boat tossed about by the breaking waves; having gone [astray], they are utterly lost. Those who hold such views must likewise be seen as fallen into false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*), saying:
"There is no gift, there is no oblation, there are no sacrifices, there are no brahmins; there is neither merit nor demerit, and there is no fruit of action. As it has been said:
"Emptiness was taught by the Victors as the relinquishing of all views;
but those for whom emptiness itself is a view were declared to be incurable."

Free from the stain of the entire web of conceptual constructions—such as the grasped and the grasper, or the one and the many—he perceives the nature of appearances, which are like a dream, an illusion, a mirage, or a city of the Gandharvas, as being the form of the maṇḍala-circle. Even while dwelling in a house and surrounded by women, by enjoying the five objects of desire whose nature is the five Buddhas purified by the five wisdoms, he fully equals all the offerings made to the Sugatas, honoring himself and others alike.

A yogi who is well-composed while performing activities such as reading scriptures or making offerings at caityas shall realize *samyaksaṃbodhi*—which consists of the three bodies (*kāyatraya*) and is capable of accomplishing all that is to be done.

[4] In the Pāramitā system, however, even after many eons, the attainment of the three bodies does not constitute *samyaksaṃbodhi*. Even for a beginner, if he always dwells in solitude, is single-mindedly devoted to the stainless samādhi of wisdom and skillful means, is devoted to the guru, and strictly observes the commitments (*samaya*) and vows (*saṃvara*), he should not perform activities such as reading scriptures at all.

Is it that perfect enlightenment cannot be accomplished apart from the cultivation of the maṇḍala-circle consisting of the three samādhis? Who here would be capable of speaking with such reasoned application? As for those who are ignorant and unlearned—who, having obtained a mere fragment of instruction, stand like fruitless trees at the top of a branch, [yet] are like clouds of water [in their capacity to provide relief]—[there are others who are] profoundly learned, upholders of the Dharma, rich in wisdom, heroes endowed with complete ethical discipline, virtuous, disciplined, and whose minds are free from self-exaltation...

Even that which is contrary [to the truth], when practiced by foolish people, they proceed to adopt as the very best, O noble one, just as in the *Karpūralatā-kathā*. Those appointed to guard the *karpūralatā*—the boatmen and ferrymen of the Sāmanatīrtha—being unable to remain there because of its fragrance, stand with their noses pressed against the tips of their fingers. For this very reason it is said that the foul odor of the hide does not trouble the leather-worker. They delight in the Buddha’s teaching, which is peaceful, fragrant, glorious, beautiful, and delightful.

Flies do not simply fall into a lotus grove; even attaining the path for entering the city of the Asuras is difficult. Even if it should somehow happen for some, then some arrive having gone by a wrong path; some remain stuck in the mud; for some, a multitude of obstacles (*māra*) of many kinds assails them; and only a few enter without contradiction. In the same way, the entry into the city of supreme stainless bliss through wisdom and means (*prajñopāya*) should be understood.
“Even a mere portion of what is to be attained is difficult to obtain,” so it was said by the Blessed One; how much more so the practice of the mantra-conduct? As it has been stated:
“Does the appearance of those who possess all-knowledge ever occur in the world, or not? It may happen only once in a great while, like the flower of the udumbara tree.”
"Even more difficult than that is the arising of the way of mantra practice,
by which one is indeed able to perform incomparable benefit for sentient beings without passing into nirvāṇa.
Having thus composed this lamp of reasoning for those who have fallen onto wrong paths, [he said:]
May all beings become like clouds that rain down the merit I have obtained from those who were shrouded in darkness by the gloom of false pride.
